title: Nahum

stories.title: 🧑‍⚖️ Nahum 1
summaryBullets: This is the burden against Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite: (1:1).
The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and full of wrath. The LORD takes vengeance on His foes and reserves wrath for His enemies. (1:2).
The LORD is slow to anger and great in power; the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. His path is in the whirlwind and storm, and clouds are the dust beneath His feet. (1:3).
He rebukes the sea and dries it up; He makes all the rivers run dry. Bashan and Carmel wither, and the flower of Lebanon wilts. (1:4).
The mountains quake before Him, and the hills melt away; the earth trembles at His presence— the world and all its dwellers. (1:5).
Who can withstand His indignation? Who can endure His burning anger? His wrath is poured out like fire; even rocks are shattered before Him. (1:6).
The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him. (1:7).
But with an overwhelming flood He will make an end of Nineveh and pursue His enemies into darkness. (1:8).
Whatever you plot against the LORD, He will bring to an end. Affliction will not rise up a second time. (1:9).
For they will be entangled as with thorns and consumed like the drink of a drunkard — like stubble that is fully dry. (1:10).
From you, O Nineveh, comes forth a plotter of evil against the LORD, a counselor of wickedness. (1:11).
This is what the LORD says: “Though they are allied and numerous, yet they will be cut down and pass away. Though I have afflicted you, O Judah, I will afflict you no longer. (1:12).
For I will now break their yoke from your neck and tear away your shackles.” (1:13).

The LORD has issued a command concerning you, O Nineveh: “There will be no descendants to carry on your name. I will cut off the carved image and cast idol from the house of your gods; I will prepare your grave, for you are contemptible.” (1:14).

Look to the mountains— the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace! Celebrate your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows. For the wicked will never again march through you; they will be utterly cut off. (1:15).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:6-7: Slow to anger yet does not clear the guilty.
Isaiah 52:7: “Good news… feet on the mountains” (shared wording).
2 Kings 19:35-37: Assyria’s earlier setback in Judah (background to God breaking the yoke).
Jonah 3:10-4:1: Earlier mercy to Nineveh; Nahum announces later judgment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַנָּא (qannāʾ, ‘zealous/jealous’), Greek (LXX): ζηλωτής, Aramaic: קנאה (qināʾā)
translationNotes.note: In 1:2 this means covenant zeal for exclusive loyalty, not petty envy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָעוֹז (maʿoz), Greek (LXX): καταφυγή, Aramaic: מעוזא (maʿozā)
translationNotes.note: Place of protection for those who trust Him (1:7).

translationNotes.term: Affliction will not rise a second time
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא תָקוּם פְּעָמַיִם (lo taqūm peʿamayim), Greek (LXX): οὐ μὴ ἀναστῇ δὶς, Aramaic: לָא תְקוּם תַּרְתֵּין
translationNotes.note: Formula of finality against Nineveh’s threat (1:9). Not a blanket promise that Judah will never suffer again in history.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְבַשֵּׂר (mevasser), Greek (LXX): εὐαγγελιζόμενος, Aramaic: מְבַשְּׂרָא (mevasserā)
translationNotes.note: The herald’s feet on the mountains (1:15) announce Nineveh’s end and Judah’s relief.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nahum opens by declaring God’s fierce justice and steady goodness: Nineveh’s end is decreed, and Judah is told to take heart.

stories.title: 🧱 Nahum 2
summaryBullets: One who scatters advances against you, O Nineveh. Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Brace yourselves! Summon all your strength! (2:1).
For the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob like the splendor of Israel, though destroyers have laid them waste and ruined the branches of their vine. (2:2).

The shields of his mighty men are red; the valiant warriors are dressed in scarlet. The fittings of the chariots flash like fire on the day they are prepared, and the spears of cypress have been brandished. (2:3).
The chariots dash through the streets; they rush around the plazas, appearing like torches, darting about like lightning. (2:4).
He summons his nobles; they stumble as they advance. They race to its wall; the protective shield is set in place. (2:5).
The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses. (2:6).
It is decreed that the city be exiled and carried away; her maidservants moan like doves, and beat upon their breasts. (2:7).
Nineveh has been like a pool of water throughout her days, but now it is draining away. “Stop! Stop!” they cry, but no one turns back. (2:8).
“Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold!” There is no end to the treasure, an abundance of every precious thing. (2:9).
She is emptied! Yes , she is desolate and laid waste! Hearts melt, knees knock, bodies tremble, and every face grows pale! (2:10).
Where is the lions’ lair or the feeding ground of the young lions, where the lion and lioness prowled with their cubs, with nothing to frighten them away? (2:11).
The lion mauled enough for its cubs and strangled prey for the lioness. It filled its dens with the kill, and its lairs with mauled prey. (2:12).

“Behold, I am against you,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will reduce your chariots to cinders, and the sword will devour your young lions. I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voices of your messengers will no longer be heard.” (2:13).
crossRefs: Isaiah 37:33-35: God’s defense against Assyria (Assyrian war backdrop).
Psalm 46:4-6: River and city imagery in siege contexts.
Hosea 13:7-8: Lion imagery used of judgment (predator motif inverted).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵפִיץ (mēfīts), Greek (LXX): διασκορπίζων, Aramaic: מְפִיץ (mefīts)
translationNotes.note: Title for the attacker who breaks Nineveh (2:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעֲרֵי הַנָּהָר (shaʿarē ha-nāhar), Greek (LXX): πύλαι ποταμοῦ, Aramaic: תרי דנהרא
translationNotes.note: A breach by water fits known siege tactics/context (2:6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֻצַּב (huttsav, “fixed/established”), Greek (LXX): ἀπεκαλύφθη/ἀνήχθη (uncovered/led away), Aramaic (Tg): אִתְגְּזַר (itgezar, “decreed”)
translationNotes.note: 2:7 is textually difficult. Likely states the fall is decreed; some older readings took it as a proper name (“Huzzab”).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְעוֹן אֲרָיוֹת (meʿon ʾarayot), Greek (LXX): κατοίκησις λεόντων, Aramaic: מדור אריין
translationNotes.note: Nineveh pictured as a predator’s lair now emptied (2:11-12).

stories.keyTakeaway: Nahum paints Nineveh’s fall in fast-cut combat scenes: river gates open, plunderers swarm, and God Himself declares, “I am against you.”

stories.title: 🩸 Nahum 3
summaryBullets: Woe to the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey. (3:1).
The crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheel, galloping horse and bounding chariot! (3:2).
Charging horseman, flashing sword, shining spear; heaps of slain, mounds of corpses, dead bodies without end— they stumble over their dead— (3:3).
because of the many harlotries of the harlot, the seductive mistress of sorcery, who betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft. (3:4).
“Behold, I am against you,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms. (3:5).
I will pelt you with filth and treat you with contempt; I will make a spectacle of you. (3:6).
Then all who see you will recoil from you and say, ‘Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?’ Where can I find comforters for you?” (3:7).
Are you better than Thebes, stationed by the Nile with water around her, whose rampart was the sea, whose wall was the water? (3:8).
Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength; Put and Libya were her allies. (3:9).
Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity. Her infants were dashed to pieces at the head of every street. They cast lots for her dignitaries, and all her nobles were bound in chains. (3:10).
You too will become drunk; you will go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy. (3:11).
All your fortresses are fig trees with the first ripe figs; when shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater! (3:12).
Look at your troops — they are like your women! The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire consumes their bars. (3:13).
Draw your water for the siege; strengthen your fortresses. Work the clay and tread the mortar; repair the brick kiln! (3:14).
There the fire will devour you; the sword will cut you down and consume you like a young locust. Make yourself many like the young locust; make yourself many like the swarming locust! (3:15).
You have multiplied your merchants more than the stars of the sky. The young locust strips the land and flies away. (3:16).
Your guards are like the swarming locust, and your scribes like clouds of locusts that settle on the walls on a cold day. When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where. (3:17).
O king of Assyria, your shepherds slumber; your officers sleep. Your people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them. (3:18).
There is no healing for your injury; your wound is severe. All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall, for who has not experienced your constant cruelty? (3:19).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 24:7-9: Bloodguilt imagery for a violent city.
Isaiah 23; Jeremiah 46: Oracles against major cities/empires.

Nahum 3:8: Thebes, called No-Amon, is held up as the precedent for Nineveh's fall. The Egyptian capital sat on the Nile with water for a wall, and Assyria sacked it anyway in 663 BC, within living memory of Nahum's hearers.
Revelation 18:2-8: Later taunt over a corrupt city’s collapse (literary parallel).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִיר דָּמִים (ʿir damim), Greek (LXX): πόλις αἱμάτων, Aramaic: קרת דמים (qart damīn)
translationNotes.note: Direct charge of murder and violence (3:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זְנוּנִים (zenunim) / כְּשָׁפִים (keshafim), Greek (LXX): πορνεῖαι / φαρμακεῖαι, Aramaic: זנונין / כשופין
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for imperial seduction/exploitation and also literal occult practices (3:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְגִלִּיתִי שׁוּלַיִךְ (ve-gillītī shūlayikh), Greek (LXX): ἀνακαλύψω τὰ ὀπίσω σου, Aramaic: אגלי בתרתיך
translationNotes.note: Stock Ancient Near Eastern judgment image of exposing an abusive city/empire (3:5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֹא אָמוֹן (No-ʾAmon), Greek (LXX): Διόςπολις/Θῆβαι, Aramaic: נא אמון
translationNotes.note: Egyptian capital on the Nile used as a precedent for a “secure” city that still fell (3:8-10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵין כֵּהָה לִשְׁבָרֵךְ (ʾein kehah lišbarekh), Greek (LXX): οὐκ ἔστιν ἴασις τῷ συντρίμματί σου, Aramaic: לֵית אֲסְוָתָא לִשְׁבָרֵךְ

stories.keyTakeaway: Nineveh is condemned for bloodshed, lies, plunder, and occult practices. Her humiliation is public and final; there is no cure for her wound.

intro:
Nahum was written by Nahum the Elkoshite (Nahum 1:1), the prophet from the town of Elkosh in Judah. The book was composed between two anchored historical events: the fall of Thebes (Hebrew: No-Amon, the capital of upper Egypt) to the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in 663 BC, which Nahum references as a past event ("Are you better than Thebes that sat by the Nile?", Nahum 3:8), and the destruction of Nineveh by a Babylonian-Median coalition in 612 BC, which Nahum prophesies as a future event throughout the book. This places the composition between roughly 663 BC and 654 BC, most likely during the reign of King Manasseh of Judah (697-642 BC), though it could fall as late as the reigns of his son Amon (642-640 BC) or the early years of his grandson Josiah (640-609 BC). Nahum was from Elkosh, a town whose exact location is debated; the most likely identification is a village in the Shephelah of southern Judah (variously called Elcesi), not far from the home of the prophet Micah a century earlier. Other traditions have placed Elkosh in Galilee near Tiberias, at Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee (whose Hebrew name Kfar Nahum literally means "village of Nahum"), or at El-Kauze near Mosul in modern Iraq (a long-standing Eastern Christian tradition). The prophet's name Nachum (נַחוּם) means "comfort" or "consolation," from the same Hebrew verbal root nacham as the longer name Nehemiah ("Yahuah comforts"). Nahum is the only prophet of this name in the Old Testament; he is distinct from Nahum mentioned in Luke 3:25 as an ancestor of Jesus, an otherwise unknown post-exilic figure with the same Hebrew name.

The historical setting is the height of Neo-Assyrian power under Ashurbanipal (669-631 BC) and his immediate successors. Ashurbanipal had conquered Egypt and sacked Thebes (No-Amon) in 663 BC, the southernmost point of Assyrian conquest, and the empire stretched from the Nile to the Persian Gulf. Manasseh of Judah (697-642 BC) was a tributary vassal of Assyria for most of his reign and is named in Ashurbanipal's cylinder inscriptions among the tributary kings of the western provinces; according to 2 Chronicles 33:11-13, Manasseh was at one point taken in chains to Babylon (probably as part of Assyrian discipline, since Ashurbanipal held court there as well) and later repented, was restored to his throne, and reformed his idolatrous practices. Nineveh, on the east bank of the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, was at its architectural peak: Sennacherib had built the "Palace Without Rival" there at the end of the 8th century BC, and the city held the great royal library that Ashurbanipal would expand and that would yield the Babylonian creation epics, the Gilgamesh tablets, and tens of thousands of administrative documents when archaeologists excavated the site in the 19th century. Less than a generation after Nahum's prophecy, Assyria collapsed catastrophically: Ashurbanipal died around 631 BC, civil war broke out, the Babylonians under Nabopolassar declared independence in 626 BC, allied with the Medes under Cyaxares, and together they captured Asshur in 614 BC and then Nineveh itself in 612 BC, leaving the city in ruins so complete that when the Greek mercenary Xenophon marched past the site two centuries later (recorded in his Anabasis), he did not realize a great city had ever stood there.

Nahum is the thirty-fourth book of the Christian Old Testament and the seventh of the twelve Minor Prophets. The Hebrew name Nachum (נַחוּם) is the prophet's own name. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Nahum were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; Qumran cave 4 also yielded a separate Hebrew commentary on Nahum (4QpNahum, "the Pesher on Nahum"), which applies the prophet's oracles to events of the Hasmonean period in the 1st century BC. Nahum's brief comfort to oppressed Judah at Nahum 1:15 ("Behold, on the mountains, the feet of him who brings good news") closely echoes Isaiah 52:7, written a century earlier; Paul quotes Isaiah's wording in Romans 10:15 to describe the preaching of the gospel.
